title: Any Saint may aid any need; particular patrons arise from craft, death, gifts, miracles, or name-play
source_text: L. Monent tamen ejus Ecclesiae Doctores omnes Sanctos aequaliter pro quibuscunque necessitatibus intercedere posse; & liberum esse singulis fidelibus ad singulos Sanctos recurrere, ut eorum ope atque auxilio quaelibet bona sibi necessaria impetrent. Nec putandum Deum inter Sanctos sic officia divisisse, ut unius rei cura huic, aut illi demandata sit, aliis vero minime: Sed ad unum potius Sanctorum, quam ad alium, ab hominibus hujus, aut illius gentis & professionis, & in his atque illis necessitatibus recurri occasione sumpta, vel ex arte & professione quam exercuisse Sancti perhibentur; vel ex supplicii & mortis genere, quo vitam suam gloriose clauserunt, vel ex singularibus gratiae divinae donis, quibus eminuerunt, vel ex insigni aliquo miraculo, sive ante mortem, sive post mortem ab ipsis patrato, sive etiam simpliciter ex quadam vocum & nominum allusione & affinitate. Ut, exempli causa, Lucam Medici sibi patronum delegerunt, quia Medicinam ipse exercuit. Et qui navigant ad Paulum, & Nicolaum confugiunt, quia in gratiam Pauli, Deus ex naufragio servavit animas ducentas & septuaginta sex qui cum ipso navigabant; & similiter quia ad preces Nicolai Episcopi Myrensis Deus miraculose navem a naufragio servasse perhibetur. Ut videre est apud Cardinalem Perronium, in refutatione responsionis Regis Magnae Britanniae lib. 5. cap. 3. Et etiam apud Jaubertum Archiepiscopum Arelatensem tom. 2. contra Molinei Clypeum, c. 1. Sect. 24.
pass_a_gloss: Yet the Doctors of that Church warn that all Saints can equally intercede for any necessities whatsoever; and that it is free for individual faithful to have recourse to individual Saints, that by their help and aid they may obtain whatever goods are necessary for themselves. Nor is it to be thought that God has so divided offices among the Saints that care of one thing has been committed to this one or that, but not at all to others: But rather that men of this or that nation and profession, and in these and those necessities, take occasion to have recourse to one of the Saints rather than to another, either from the art and profession which the Saints are reported to have exercised; or from the kind of punishment and death by which they gloriously closed their life, or from singular gifts of divine grace in which they excelled, or from some notable miracle wrought by them either before or after death, or even simply from a certain allusion and affinity of words and names. As, for example’s sake, Physicians chose Luke as patron for themselves because he himself practiced Medicine. And those who sail flee to Paul and Nicholas, because for Paul’s sake God saved from shipwreck two hundred and seventy-six souls who were sailing with him; and likewise because at the prayers of Nicholas Bishop of Myra God is reported to have miraculously saved a ship from shipwreck. As may be seen in Cardinal Perron, in the refutation of the King of Great Britain’s response, book 5, chapter 3. And also in Jaubert Archbishop of Arles, volume 2, against Molina’s Shield, chapter 1, section 24.
pass_b_english: Any Saint can intercede for any need; the faithful may approach any.
God did not fence offices so tightly—patrons stick by craft, martyrdom, gifts, miracles, or even name-affinity.
Luke for medicine; Paul and Nicholas for seafarers (Acts shipwreck; Myra miracle).

choices.term: nec putandum Deum inter Sanctos sic officia divisisse
choices.english: nor is God to be thought to have so divided offices among the Saints
choices.why: Balances XLIX’s patron custom against universal capacity.
